title: What is HELUT?
youtubeTitle: What is HELUT? Living Research on Circuits, Torus FHE, and TensorLUT
description: A plain-language map of HELUT: one Yosys-to-Metal compiler substrate, two core research paths, chosen application case studies, and a living claim ledger that gets corrected in public. Epoch C69. Site: https://helut.digitaldefiance.org · Source: https://github.com/Digital-Defiance/HELUT

scenes.headline: What is HELUT?
scenes.subhead: Living research · living silicon · a dated ledger
scenes.voiceover: This is living research on living silicon. Every claim in this series carries a date, because the ledger changes as evidence arrives. HELUT stands for Homomorphic Edge Look-Up Tensors: a Swift and Metal research prototype that treats a digital circuit as something you can compute, search, and encrypt on Apple silicon.

scenes.headline: A substrate, not one application
bullets: Yosys netlist: wires, look-up tables, flip-flops
Many independent circuit instances in one batch
scenes.voiceover: Yosys is an open-source synthesis tool. It turns a circuit description into a parts list called a netlist: wires, look-up tables, and flip-flops. A look-up table stores a small truth table, which lists the output for every possible input. HELUT compiles those supported parts, adds a batch dimension for independent circuit instances, and runs them on Metal. Once a problem fits that shape, it can become a case study.

scenes.headline: Torus FHE · TensorLUT
scenes.subhead: Applications use it without redefining it.
scenes.voiceover: The Metal compiler is shared infrastructure. One core research path evaluates circuit wires under torus fully homomorphic encryption. Another, TensorLUT, searches the truth tables that define hardware. The cleartext compiler and batch engine also power concrete applications. Later in this series, I show one I chose: using historical Enigma as a difficult search problem. That application does not define HELUT.

scenes.headline: What runs today
bullets: Supported Yosys circuits → CPU and Metal graphs
Cleartext batches, encrypted LUTs, TensorLUT search
Application case studies keep separate claims
scenes.voiceover: Today the repository compiles supported Yosys circuits to CPU and Metal graphs. It runs cleartext batches, encrypted look-up-table demonstrations, and TensorLUT synthesis experiments. It has also booted a processor core under encryption, one clock tick at a time. I used the cleartext batch path for the P1030680 Enigma campaign, and a later rotor-inspired experiment called E256 grew out of it.

scenes.headline: The non-claims are part of the result
bullets: No claim to have invented torus FHE
scenes.voiceover: HELUT did not invent torus fully homomorphic encryption. In the Enigma application, it has not decrypted P1030680. The later E256 offshoot is not approved for real secrets, and cross-implementation parity is not a security proof. Even the hardness estimates are configuration-specific: of eight compared parameter sets, only four agree with the reference estimator inside the stated tolerance.

scenes.headline: Deliberately unfinished
scenes.voiceover: This project is deliberately unfinished. The claim sheet is a living ledger: results get measured again, and some get withdrawn. One encrypted failure turned out to be a nondeterminism bug rather than a limit. Seven timing rows had understated the code by about two times. The work is a search for new levers, new applications, and better evidence. When a claim breaks, it gets fixed in public, with the correction recorded.

scenes.headline: Next: the compiler substrate
scenes.subhead: One Yosys circuit, from JSON to a Metal graph.
scenes.voiceover: Next, we follow one supported Yosys circuit from JSON into a Metal graph. That shared compiler makes the later cleartext, encrypted, and TensorLUT paths easier to understand.
